screens.title: The SysOps role in detection and response
screens.narratorSegment: As a SysOps Administrator your responsibility goes beyond deploying preventative controls. You must actively monitor for signs of compromise, triage findings, and participate in containment and remediation. Detection means collecting signals from logs and analytics; triage means deciding severity and next steps; containment means limiting damage while preserving evidence. For example, when an EC2 instance shows sustained outbound connections to known malicious IPs, detection tools surface the event, triage marks it as high severity, and containment might involve modifying security group rules and taking a snapshot for forensics. A common misconception is that detection tools alone solve security. They don't — they surface findings that must be interpreted, prioritized, and acted upon. Another misconception is that automation always reduces risk; poorly tested automation can cause outages. Practice: assign clear responsibilities, classify findings by impact, and run tabletop exercises. Key signals you'll rely on include A P I activity, VPC flow patterns, DNS anomalies, and configuration drift. The core insight is that prevention and detection are complementary: prevention reduces incidents, but detection and measured response reduce impact when incidents occur. Which signals will you tune first in your environment?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › SysOps Role
Definition & responsibilities

SysOps administrators monitor environments, interpret security findings, perform containment steps, and ensure forensic data is preserved for investigation.

Detection
Collect logs and alerts from GuardDuty, Config, and other sources.
Triage
Assess severity and decide whether to escalate or contain.
Containment
Isolate resources, snapshot forensics, and preserve logs.
Concrete example
Compromised EC2 instance
GuardDuty finds high outbound traffic to a malicious IP. Triage marks it high. Containment steps: revoke instance access, modify security group to block outbound traffic, snapshot attached EBS volume for forensics, stop the instance.
Key Takeaway

Detection without triage and containment leaves incidents unresolved. Plan both people and pre-approved automation for fast, safe response.

screens.title: AWS GuardDuty — continuous intelligent detection
screens.narratorSegment: AWS GuardDuty provides continuous threat detection by analyzing multiple data sources for suspicious patterns. It ingests VPC Flow Logs to understand network flows, CloudTrail management and S3 data event logs for A P I activity and object access, and DNS logs for domains and lookups. GuardDuty applies machine learning, anomaly detection, and integrated threat intelligence feeds to prioritize findings such as compromised EC2 instances running malware, unauthorized access to S3 objects, A P I calls from unusual locations, and port scanning attempts. Importantly, GuardDuty is agentless — it does not require installing additional software on your instances — which simplifies deployment. A practical example: a sudden spike in outbound connections combined with unusual A P I calls can lead GuardDuty to produce a high-severity finding that includes resource identifiers and recommended actions. A common misconception is treating every finding as an incident; findings are signals that require triage. Another is that GuardDuty replaces log retention — it complements your logs and points you to what to investigate. The key is to use findings as prioritized leads, not the final verdict, and to integrate them with your central workflow.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › GuardDuty
What GuardDuty analyzes
  • VPC Flow Logs — network traffic patterns and unusual flows.
  • CloudTrail management and S3 data events — API calls and object access.
  • DNS logs — suspicious domain lookups or exfiltration signals.
Sample findings
Compromised EC2 performing cryptomining
Unauthorized S3 access or exposed bucket
API calls from unusual geographical locations
Why agentless matters

Agentless detection reduces operational effort and speeds rollout across accounts because you do not need to install and maintain agents on every host. GuardDuty evaluates central logs and telemetry instead.

Triage advice
  • Check resource identifiers and timestamps on the finding.
  • Correlate with Config and CloudTrail records for recent configuration changes and API activity.
  • Use severity and type to decide containment steps and escalation.
Key Takeaway

Treat GuardDuty findings as prioritized leads. Use them to guide investigation and, when validated, to trigger notifications or remediation flows.

screens.title: GuardDuty findings: content and integrations
screens.narratorSegment: GuardDuty findings include structured details: a finding type, severity, affected resource ARNs, timestamps, and contextual evidence. You will typically see severity levels that guide triage and a description that explains why the finding was raised. Integrations are critical: findings can be sent to Security Hub for centralized prioritization, to EventBridge for automation, or to third-party SIEMs for longer analysis. A typical automated flow sends a finding to EventBridge where a rule routes specific types to an SNS topic for paging the on-call team and another rule triggers a Lambda for pre-approved remediation when the finding is high severity. Important practical advice: avoid acting on findings until you validate them to prevent false positives from causing unnecessary disruption. Use sample findings and historical data to tune alerts and suppression rules. Another practical item is mapping findings to runbooks: attach a recommended action set to each high-severity finding type. This makes response repeatable and reduces cognitive load during incidents. How would you map findings to your existing escalation steps? In practical terms, understanding finding details and how to forward them for action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Findings & Integrations
Finding anatomy
  • Type and description explaining the suspicious activity.
  • Severity score used to prioritize response.
  • Affected resources and timestamps for context.
  • Evidence such as IPs, domains, and API calls.
Where findings go
Security Hub for aggregation and compliance mapping.
EventBridge to trigger notifications or Lambda functions.
SIEM for long-term analysis and correlation.
Example automated flow
High-severity EC2 compromise
GuardDuty finding → EventBridge rule filters by type and severity → SNS notifies on-call team → Lambda (in sandbox) isolates instance and snapshots volume if runbook conditions match.
Tuning tips
  • Create suppression or exception lists to reduce false positives.
  • Use historical patterns to refine severity thresholds and routing rules.
  • Document runbook steps and map them to finding types for rapid response.
Common mistake

Triggering irreversible actions without validation can amplify an incident. Always include gating checks or manual approval for high-impact remediations.

screens.title: AWS Security Hub — centralizing your security posture
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Security Hub provides a single place to view and prioritize security findings from GuardDuty, AWS Config, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, WAF, and supported third-party tools. It normalizes findings into a common format, maps them to industry standards like AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, and highlights high-priority issues across accounts. For a SysOps Administrator, Security Hub reduces the cognitive load of juggling multiple consoles by offering an aggregated view and automated checks. When GuardDuty generates a finding, Security Hub can ingest it and show how that finding impacts compliance status. A common misconception is assuming Security Hub automatically fixes problems; it does not — it organizes and prioritizes. Instead, integrate Security Hub with EventBridge or ticketing systems to ensure findings translate into action. Use Security Hub to create dashboards, set up insight rules for recurring problem types, and monitor trends. The key benefit is consistent prioritization and an audit trail that supports compliance and operational decision-making. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Security Hub
What Security Hub does
  • Aggregates findings from multiple AWS services and third-party products.
  • Normalizes and prioritizes findings for consistent triage.
  • Maps findings to standards and produces compliance checks.
Practical uses
Create insight rules for repeated issues.
Send prioritized findings to ticketing or EventBridge for automation.
Use compliance reports for audits and executive summaries.
Example scenario
Aggregated S3 exposures
GuardDuty and Config produce findings about public S3 buckets. Security Hub surfaces these related findings, maps them to a compliance standard, and scores the account's posture so teams can prioritize remediation for the riskiest items.
Key Takeaway

Security Hub is your single pane for security posture. Use it to prioritize findings and feed downstream workflows that turn alerts into action.

screens.title: Security Hub standards and prioritization
screens.narratorSegment: Security Hub includes automated checks against established AWS best practices and industry standards. For example, enabling AWS Foundational Security Best Practices runs a set of checks that examine account and resource configurations and then surfaces findings where your environment deviates. These checks give you an immediate compliance score and a list of prioritized issues. The practical value is twofold: first, it directs attention to misconfigurations that increase risk; second, it lets SysOps demonstrate continuous compliance to auditors and stakeholders. A common mistake is to treat Security Hub's compliance score as the only measure of security; it is a helpful indicator, but operational security also requires patching, identity hygiene, and network controls. Use Security Hub insights to create dashboards and automate escalations. For example, create an insight for public S3 exposures across accounts and route those findings to a ticketing system or EventBridge rule so you can track remediation progress. Prioritization helps you focus scarce operational time on the riskiest issues. Automated checks

Enable standards like AWS Foundational Security Best Practices to run automated configuration checks; findings map to known risks with remediation guidance.

Use cases
  • Create a compliance dashboard for leadership.
  • Drive remediation sprints by prioritized findings.
  • Feed findings to change control and ticketing systems.
Practical pattern
Insight rules + automation
Create Security Hub insights for recurring risks like public S3 exposures. Use EventBridge to route those insights into ticketing or remediation pipelines to maintain a measurable backlog.
Key Takeaway

Security Hub turns many signals into a prioritized, auditable view. Use that view to guide operational effort and to communicate risk to stakeholders.

screens.title: AWS Config — continuous configuration monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config continuously records the configuration state of your AWS resources and enables automated evaluation against desired configurations using Config rules. It keeps historical configuration snapshots so you can see drift over time and supports both managed and custom rules. For example, a managed rule like s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited checks whether S3 buckets are publicly accessible and flags non-compliant resources. Another rule might verify that EBS volumes are encrypted or that EC2 instances do not have public IPs. When Config detects non-compliance, it records the change and can trigger notifications, which helps with auditing and remediation. A common misconception is thinking Config prevents misconfiguration; it audits and alerts but does not by itself change resource settings. Use Config as the authoritative record for configuration and pair it with automated flows to remediate or notify teams. The benefit is continuous assurance: you discover drift quickly and can demonstrate compliance to auditors and internal reviewers. What Config provides
  • Continuous recording of resource configurations and snapshots over time.
  • Automated evaluation against managed or custom Config rules.
  • Non-compliance alerts that feed into incident workflows or reports.
Example rules
s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited
encrypted-volumes
ec2-instance-no-public-ip
Practical guidance

Use Config to detect drift immediately after changes, and link non-compliant events to runbooks and notification channels. Keep historical snapshots for forensic analysis and proof of remediation.

Key Takeaway

Config gives you an authoritative trail of resource state and automated rule evaluations. Use it for auditing, compliance, and feeding automated workflows.

screens.title: Config Rules — examples and evaluation
screens.narratorSegment: Config rules evaluate resource configurations and mark them as compliant or non-compliant. Managed rules like s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited come pre-built and check common risk patterns, while custom rules let you encode organization-specific policies. When a resource is created or changed, Config records the new state and evaluates the rule. If it fails, Config emits a non-compliant event, which can trigger SNS notifications or an EventBridge rule. Use the evaluation to kick off a ticket or a Lambda that re-applies encryption settings where safe to do so. Always allow Config to finish initial evaluations and check the recorded history when investigating a late alert. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Config Rules
Rule lifecycle
  1. Config records current resource state or snapshots.
  2. Rule evaluates the recorded state against expected configuration.
  3. Non-compliant results emit events for notification and action.
Example: public S3

Create the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited rule. When a bucket ACL or policy allows public-read, the rule evaluates to NON_COMPLIANT and can trigger an SNS topic for remediation tracking.

Remediation patterns
  • Notify owners and create tickets for manual review.
  • Trigger sandboxed Lambda to attempt safe configuration fixes with logging.
  • Record all changes in Config history for audit and rollback planning.
Misconception

Config does not block non-compliant changes by default. It detects drift and alerts; remediation must be implemented separately.

screens.title: Basic incident response workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A simple, repeatable incident response workflow helps you move quickly when threats appear. The flow begins with detection: GuardDuty raises a finding. EventBridge receives that finding and applies a rule that filters by type and severity. The rule can route the event to two parallel targets: an SNS topic to notify the security team and a Lambda function to run pre-approved remediation steps. For example, on a high-severity instance compromise, the Lambda could detach network interfaces, modify security groups to deny outbound traffic, snapshot attached volumes for forensics, and stop the instance. Each action must be carefully reviewed and tested in non-production so you avoid unwanted outages. Notifications should include finding details, affected resources, timestamps, and suggested next steps so humans can act if automation cannot handle a case. A common misconception is to automate too broadly; instead, use severity thresholds and gating checks like a short manual approval or a secondary verification step. The critical idea is to make response predictable, reproducible, and reversible wherever possible. Basic incident response workflow means use eventbridge to route findings to sns for alerts and lambda for gated remediation; test all automated actions in a sandbox first.. In practical terms, detection → notification → alerting → automated remediation (optional). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Four-step workflow
1. Detection — GuardDuty creates a finding.
2. Notification — EventBridge rule routes events.
3. Alerting — SNS notifies teams by email, SMS or pager.
4. Remediation — Lambda executes pre-approved actions if safe.
Concrete example
Compromised instance flow
GuardDuty finding → EventBridge rule (filters high severity) → SNS alerts on-call → Lambda creates EBS snapshot, modifies SG to isolate instance, and stops it with logs for review.
Key Takeaway

Design workflows with gates and reversible steps. Automate to reduce response time but always include human review for high-impact operations.

screens.title: Automated remediation with Lambda — patterns and precautions
screens.narratorSegment: Automated remediation often runs as AWS Lambda functions triggered by EventBridge. Typical safe actions include isolating an instance by updating its security group, creating a snapshot for forensics, or disabling access keys for an IAM user. When building a Lambda remediation, include these patterns: validate the finding and resource state before acting; require a severity threshold and a time-since-detection check; log every decision and output to CloudWatch; and include a dry-run or sandbox flag for testing. For example, a Lambda could inspect a GuardDuty finding, check if the instance is in a test account or has a test tag, and only then proceed to create a snapshot and adjust network rules. A frequent misconception is that a single remediation function fits all scenarios; instead design small functions with well-defined scopes and explicit rollback steps. Remember to instrument the function with metrics and alerts so you can detect failed remediation attempts or unexpected side effects. The main idea is to automate predictable, reversible actions and ensure visibility and control when automation runs. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Lambda Remediation
Remediation checklist
  • Confirm the finding's resource and severity before acting.
  • Enforce sandbox or test tags for automatic actions.
  • Create snapshots and log metadata for forensic needs.
  • Provide rollback steps and metrics for success/failure.
Small code example (conceptual)
def handler(event, context):
  # Validate severity and resource tag
  finding = event['detail']
  if finding['severity'] < 6:
    return 'Ignored: low severity'
  # Check for test account tag
  if not is_test_resource(finding['resource']):
    return 'Requires manual review'
  snapshot_volume(finding['resource'])
  isolate_instance(finding['resource'])
  log_action(finding)
Precautions
  • Use least-privilege IAM roles for Lambda.
  • Include dry-run modes and manual gates for production.
  • Test thoroughly in sandbox accounts with representative data.
Pro tip

Design small, single-purpose remediations that are auditable and reversible. Monitor their metrics and failures closely.

screens.title: EventBridge and SNS — routing, filtering, and alerting
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon EventBridge acts as an event bus that receives GuardDuty findings and routes them using rules. Rules can filter on detail fields such as finding type and severity, enabling precise routing. Common targets include SNS topics for human notification and Lambda for automated remediation. SNS delivers messages via email, SMS, or push to paging systems, ensuring the right team is notified quickly. When designing these integrations, use rule-level filtering to avoid noisy notifications and include context in messages: include finding ID, affected resource ARNs, timestamps, and recommended next steps. A misconception is forwarding all findings verbatim to on-call teams; instead aggregate or suppress low-severity findings and create escalation tiers. For automation, use EventBridge to fan-out to multiple targets — for example, notify humans while also invoking a sandboxed Lambda that runs safe checks. Ensure IAM policies restrict who can modify EventBridge rules and SNS topics so attackers cannot modify routing. The main idea is to use EventBridge and SNS as reliable, auditable plumbing that connects detection to people and automation without overwhelming either. EventBridge and SNS — routing, filtering, and alerting means use eventbridge rules to filter findings and route them to sns for alerts and lambda for controlled automation, with gating and audit controls.. Routing pattern

  • Filter on severity thresholds to reduce noise.

screens.title: Shared responsibility and proactive operations
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the shared responsibility model is essential for incident response. AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud — the physical infrastructure, hypervisor, and global services. You are responsible for security in the cloud — configuring EC2 instances, S3 buckets, IAM policies, and responding to incidents that involve your resources. Practically, this means you must enable and configure services like GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Config and ensure their outputs map to your operational practices. Proactive detection goes beyond enabling services: regularly review findings, tune rules to your environment, and run tabletop exercises. A common misconception is assuming AWS will flag every risky configuration or malicious action for you; those services provide signals, but you must interpret them and act. Another important practice: maintain a cadence for reviewing findings, remove obsolete suppression rules, and update runbooks as new threat patterns emerge. The actionable insight is to pair cloud provider protections with your operational processes and continuous improvement so detection and response become routine rather than ad hoc. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how AWS helps you detect threats continuously, aggregate findings in a central dashboard, and take automated, pre-approved actions when incidents occur. We focus on three cornerstone services: GuardDuty for intelligent threat detection, Security Hub for aggregating and prioritizing findings, and AWS Config for auditing resource configurations. Together they form a proactive security cycle: detect, notify, evaluate, and optionally remediate. I will also show a practical incident response workflow using EventBridge, SNS, and Lambda so you can automate alerts and fast containment steps. For example, GuardDuty can surface an EC2 instance that is suddenly mining cryptocurrency; Security Hub can rank that as high severity, and an EventBridge rule can trigger a Lambda function that isolates the instance. Throughout, remember the shared responsibility model: AWS protects the infrastructure, you protect your configurations and respond to findings. By the end of this chapter you’ll understand what each service does, how they integrate, and how to test a basic response safely. Ask yourself: what would you automate, and what should remain a human decision?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how GuardDuty provides continuous, agentless threat detection and why that matters for quick detection of compromised resources. You will also be able to use Security Hub to aggregate findings across services and prioritize them using built-in standards. Further, you will configure AWS Config rules to audit and enforce resource settings and understand how to test those rules. Finally, you will describe a basic incident response workflow using EventBridge, SNS, and Lambda to notify teams and optionally execute safe remediation steps. Each objective links a conceptual skill with a practical action: detection, consolidation, compliance, and response. As you work through the exercises, practice enabling services in test accounts and generating sample findings so you can observe the end-to-end cycle. Keep the shared responsibility model in mind: AWS manages infrastructure security, and you manage configuration and incident response for your resources. These objectives help you move from awareness to practical, tested operations.

This second objectives slide focuses on safe practice: enabling services in non-production accounts, generating sample findings, and testing automated responses. You should be able to enable GuardDuty and Security Hub, then generate or view sample findings to understand the data they provide. You will also create a simple AWS Config rule, observe its evaluations, and safely generate a non-compliant resource to confirm the detection. Importantly, you will design one automated remediation action but only test it in a sandbox environment. Automated remediation speeds response but can inadvertently cause outages, so we emphasize testing with pre-approved actions and clear rollback plans. This objective pairs hands-on skills with operational caution: know where detection comes from, how to read findings, and how to safely practice responses. By the end, you will have run the short lab to see GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Config work together and reflected on what remediation should be automated versus manual.

As a SysOps Administrator your responsibility goes beyond deploying preventative controls. You must actively monitor for signs of compromise, triage findings, and participate in containment and remediation. Detection means collecting signals from logs and analytics; triage means deciding severity and next steps; containment means limiting damage while preserving evidence. For example, when an EC2 instance shows sustained outbound connections to known malicious IPs, detection tools surface the event, triage marks it as high severity, and containment might involve modifying security group rules and taking a snapshot for forensics. A common misconception is that detection tools alone solve security. They don't — they surface findings that must be interpreted, prioritized, and acted upon. Another misconception is that automation always reduces risk; poorly tested automation can cause outages. Practice: assign clear responsibilities, classify findings by impact, and run tabletop exercises. Key signals you'll rely on include A P I activity, VPC flow patterns, DNS anomalies, and configuration drift. The core insight is that prevention and detection are complementary: prevention reduces incidents, but detection and measured response reduce impact when incidents occur. Which signals will you tune first in your environment?

AWS GuardDuty provides continuous threat detection by analyzing multiple data sources for suspicious patterns. It ingests VPC Flow Logs to understand network flows, CloudTrail management and S3 data event logs for A P I activity and object access, and DNS logs for domains and lookups. GuardDuty applies machine learning, anomaly detection, and integrated threat intelligence feeds to prioritize findings such as compromised EC2 instances running malware, unauthorized access to S3 objects, A P I calls from unusual locations, and port scanning attempts. Importantly, GuardDuty is agentless — it does not require installing additional software on your instances — which simplifies deployment. A practical example: a sudden spike in outbound connections combined with unusual A P I calls can lead GuardDuty to produce a high-severity finding that includes resource identifiers and recommended actions. A common misconception is treating every finding as an incident; findings are signals that require triage. Another is that GuardDuty replaces log retention — it complements your logs and points you to what to investigate. The key is to use findings as prioritized leads, not the final verdict, and to integrate them with your central workflow.

GuardDuty findings include structured details: a finding type, severity, affected resource ARNs, timestamps, and contextual evidence. You will typically see severity levels that guide triage and a description that explains why the finding was raised. Integrations are critical: findings can be sent to Security Hub for centralized prioritization, to EventBridge for automation, or to third-party SIEMs for longer analysis. A typical automated flow sends a finding to EventBridge where a rule routes specific types to an SNS topic for paging the on-call team and another rule triggers a Lambda for pre-approved remediation when the finding is high severity. Important practical advice: avoid acting on findings until you validate them to prevent false positives from causing unnecessary disruption. Use sample findings and historical data to tune alerts and suppression rules. Another practical item is mapping findings to runbooks: attach a recommended action set to each high-severity finding type. This makes response repeatable and reduces cognitive load during incidents. How would you map findings to your existing escalation steps? GuardDuty findings: content and integrations means findings contain structured evidence and should be routed to security hub, eventbridge, or siems; use rules and runbooks to automate validated responses.. In practical terms, understanding finding details and how to forward them for action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Security Hub provides a single place to view and prioritize security findings from GuardDuty, AWS Config, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, WAF, and supported third-party tools. It normalizes findings into a common format, maps them to industry standards like AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, and highlights high-priority issues across accounts. For a SysOps Administrator, Security Hub reduces the cognitive load of juggling multiple consoles by offering an aggregated view and automated checks. When GuardDuty generates a finding, Security Hub can ingest it and show how that finding impacts compliance status. A common misconception is assuming Security Hub automatically fixes problems; it does not — it organizes and prioritizes. Instead, integrate Security Hub with EventBridge or ticketing systems to ensure findings translate into action. Use Security Hub to create dashboards, set up insight rules for recurring problem types, and monitor trends. The key benefit is consistent prioritization and an audit trail that supports compliance and operational decision-making. AWS Security Hub — centralizing your security posture means security hub aggregates and normalizes findings and maps them to standards so teams can prioritize corrective actions consistently.. In practical terms, aggregate, organize, and prioritize findings across services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Understanding the shared responsibility model is essential for incident response. AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud — the physical infrastructure, hypervisor, and global services. You are responsible for security in the cloud — configuring EC2 instances, S3 buckets, IAM policies, and responding to incidents that involve your resources. Practically, this means you must enable and configure services like GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Config and ensure their outputs map to your operational practices. Summarizing the essentials: GuardDuty continuously detects suspicious activity across multiple telemetry sources using machine learning and threat intelligence, and it produces findings you must triage. Security Hub aggregates those findings and maps them to standards so you can prioritize and report on security posture. Remember to test automation in non-production, keep remediation actions reversible, and treat findings as leads that require validation. Finally, understand the shared responsibility model: AWS secures the infrastructure; you secure your resources and operate the detection and response processes. Carry these core practices into your operations: enable detection, centralize findings, audit configurations, and design measured automation with human oversight.
